classification.difficultyReason: Requires a purposeful multiplying factor, expansion, a Pythagorean substitution and factor cancellation while respecting the common domain.

answer.short:
$\frac{1+\cos\theta-\sin\theta}{1+\cos\theta+\sin\theta}=\frac{\cos\theta}{1+\sin\theta}$, wherever both sides are defined.

Multiply the right-hand numerator and denominator by $1+\sin\theta$, use $1-\sin^2\theta=\cos^2\theta$, then factor and cancel.
answer.worked:
Work on the common domain, where $1+\sin\theta\ne0$ and $1+\cos\theta+\sin\theta\ne0$.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{1+\cos\theta-\sin\theta}{1+\cos\theta+\sin\theta}&=\frac{(1+\cos\theta-\sin\theta)(1+\sin\theta)}{(1+\cos\theta+\sin\theta)(1+\sin\theta)}\\\frac{1+\cos\theta-\sin\theta}{1+\cos\theta+\sin\theta}&=\frac{1+\cos\theta+\sin\theta\cos\theta-\sin^2\theta}{(1+\cos\theta+\sin\theta)(1+\sin\theta)}\\\frac{1+\cos\theta-\sin\theta}{1+\cos\theta+\sin\theta}&=\frac{\cos^2\theta+\cos\theta+\sin\theta\cos\theta}{(1+\cos\theta+\sin\theta)(1+\sin\theta)}\\\frac{1+\cos\theta-\sin\theta}{1+\cos\theta+\sin\theta}&=\frac{\cos\theta(1+\cos\theta+\sin\theta)}{(1+\cos\theta+\sin\theta)(1+\sin\theta)}\\\frac{1+\cos\theta-\sin\theta}{1+\cos\theta+\sin\theta}&=\frac{\cos\theta}{1+\sin\theta}.\end{align*}$$
This is the left-hand side, so the identity is proved wherever both sides are defined.
